### introDuction **•** **_Once again the sharp moves in the commodity markets have been triggered by developments in the United States. Federal Reserve Chairman Bernanke’s bi-annual Congressional testimony caused market participants to doubt the likelihood of QE3 and this prompted heavy liquidation and technical selling across the board. We are looking for some further mild price erosion in the precious sector during March and then consolidation in the second quarter, before a more sustained recovery emerges in the second half._** **•** **_Gold traded in a range of over $102 on 29th February, the largest intra-day band since the heavy falls of September 2011. This prompted some physical bargain hunting while taking speculative length out of the market. After rising towards $1,730 during February, gold started March below $1,700 and may slip towards $1,650 in April before building a platform for renewed gains in the second half of 2012 on fears of excessive liquidity and fiat currency risk._** **•** **_Silver was once again hugely volatile towards endFebruary, first breaking sharply upwards on technical trading and then falling in line with the rest of the sector. Prices rallied towards resistance at $38, where the market encountered physical selling, before sliding towards $34 after Dr. Bernanke’s statement. Further erosion towards $31 is likely in March and $29 in April as gold

settles. Still in surplus, silver will rely on fresh investment to boost prices and this will need the market to expect fresh gold strength._** **•** **_Platinum’s supply-side tensions, especially the strike at Impala during February, built a risk premium into the price and brought platinum almost back to partly with gold at the start of March. Possible shortfalls from Impala may take_** **_platinum back to a premium to gold in April, but we expect the discount to reappear thereafter and it could exceed $150 by year-end._** **•** **_Palladium is still the most robust metal in the sector and is the only one not to have severed its uptrend during the falls at end-February. With Russian deliveries from inventory likely to decline this year, the market will move into a residual deficit (i.e. after inventory movements are taken into account) and remain in deficit for the foreseeable future. Palladium opened March with a fix of $704; we expect it to reach $850 before the end of 2012._** ###### cOMMODiTy raNkiNG 2ND MarcH 2012 |**From 1st February 2012**|**From 1st March 20**|**11**| |---|---|---| |rhodium

Dr. Bernanke’s testimony to congress at the end of February was taken by some market participants to mean that the likelihood of a third round of quantitative easing was receding. it is certainly arguable that the falls in precious metals prices were overdone in the falls after his presentation. The extent of the losses, however, also reflect the fact that metal prices had been moving into overbought territory. The exception was palladium, which had been moving more steadily. Gold and silver had bounced higher in response to the agreement with respect to the bail-out for Greece and platinum prices were strengthening in response to the strike at impala, along with continuing concerns about platinum producers’ margins and the implication for any expansion programmes over the medium term. Dr. Bernanke’s testimony indicated that the united states’ economy is on course for modest growth this year. He argued that the first two rounds of quantitative easing, together with Operation Twist, had helped to create approximately 2.5 million jobs and that inflation in the united states was “looking for about 2%... this year”. He did, however, state in a question session in the senate that the employment situation was “far from normal” and that the high level of long-term unemployment was “particularly troubling”. The Non-Farm Payroll figures for February exceeded market expectations (and helped to support the dollar), but the long-term unemployment number (i.e. those unemployed for at least 27 weeks) has remained steady and the underemployed level is rising. These undercurrents do not automatically point to another round of easing, but the uncertainty with resp

the eu to chinese export activity. The People’s Bank of china has again cut the reserve requirement ratio for domestic banks in order to help underpin the domestic economy, and in so doing released up to $65Bn in lending capacity. This could fuel concerns about the possibility of resurgent inflation. Headline inflation in china for january was 4.5%, the first increase in five months but projected real economic growth remains in positive territory; real interest rates are negative, however, and the local population remains concerned, as alluded to above, about the possibility of resurgent inflationary forces. Widespread international uncertainty remains likely to underpin sustained gold investment and this informs our view for renewed price gains towards the end of 2012 and into early 2013, but in the near term the gold price is likely to consolidate as the physical market stabilises. **I3** March 2012 - IntroductIon confidential - not for distribution

### GOLD **•** **_Gold’s violent price action at the end of February, with a small fall in the wake of the European Central Bank’s (ECB) repurchase exercise and then a 6% fall in one extremely busy Comex trading session following Dr. Bernanke’s testimony, underpins our view that the price is due to trade at lower levels in the next few months. This is despite the fact that the fall has brought out bargain hunters, in Asia especially._** **•** **_We continue to expect gold to make new highs towards the end of the year, with the potential for the yellow metal to break through $2,000. Investment momentum should build as inflationary expectations continue to rise, while the markets remain nervous over fiat currencies._** **•** **_We are looking for gold prices to improve in the medium term despite a rising US dollar over the year as this is expected to be more a function of weakness elsewhere rather than independent dollar strength._** **•** **_At the “grass roots” level, the physical market was not robust during February, with the Indian wedding season disappointing while Chinese demand was muted after the New Year’s holiday. Some signs of scrap selling reappeared in parts of the Far East and US gold Eagle coin sales were slow. This meant that prices were vulnerable to a correction, which duly materialised._** The approach towards the $1,790 high in the final week of February was driven largely by speculative activity, combined with some short covering. While there is scope for a bounce in the wake of the end-February fall, when gold traded below $1,700, we expect prices to drift lower in the next few months, possibly dipping to as low as $1,650 during April, before starting to stabilise and form a base for a fresh, steady, gain over the rest of the year. February sentiment was cautious in the first half of the month, then started to shift. Following a test of $1,800, the sharp correction is likely to lead to a “dead cat” bounce before a downward drift In the short term, the uptrend in price has been severed and technical resistance has developed at $1,740-$1,750 (the first fix in March was $1,721.00). There is support at $1,680-$1,690 and there are some signs of investor bargain hunting in parts of Asia, including China where Shanghai Gold Exchange volumes soared at the start of March, and in India where buying reappeared soon after the price fall. We believe that any near-term bounce will be short-lived before prices

slip lower again and a test of $1,650 is likely in April before prices consolidate during the rest of the second quarter. Towards the middle of the month it was reported that the government had instructed its domestic banks to roll over their loans to local authorities. These loans form part of the domestic economic stimulus programme and it is understood that the maturities on at least some of them are now being extended in order

to avoid default before the investment projects tied to these loans are brought to fruition and start to generate a return. Soon thereafter, in the third week of February, the people’s Bank of China stated that it would, effective 24th February, reduce domestic banks’ reserve ratio requirement (rrr). This is the second such reduction; the first was at the end of november 2011, effective 5th december. The cut will take the ratio to 20.5% for the majority of large banks and it has been estimated that the cut will increase domestic lending capacity by approximately $60Bn. This move reinforces the market view that the Chinese government is now concentrating on domestic stimulus in order to bring about a soft landing, especially given the reduction in export demand as a result of the problems in Europe in particular. Although Chinese headline inflation is below 5%, the local populace remains concerned about inflationary pressures. domestic gold demand has been quiet in recent weeks and local observers are suggesting that domestic banks have substantial gold inventory (especially following high reported export levels from hong Kong to China towards the end of 2011). Even so, the macroeconomic background developing in China is prompting some bullish expectations within the gold market overall. It is arguable that $1,760 is likely to be an influential level of resistance in the near term.
